Fit a Bagged Nearest-Neighbour Survival Model

Source: R/fit_bnnsurv.R
fit_bnnsurv.Rd

Fits a bagged ensemble of k-nearest-neighbour Kaplan-Meier learners (Lowsky et al., 2013, bagged as in Wright's bnnSurvival). The engine is implemented natively in survalis.

Usage

fit_bnnsurv(
  formula,
  data,
  k = 5,
  num_base_learners = 10,
  num_features_per_base_learner = NULL,
  metric = c("mahalanobis", "euclidean"),
  weighting_function = function(x) x * 0 + 1,
  replace = TRUE,
  sample_fraction = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

A survival formula of the form Surv(time, status) ~ predictors.

data

A data frame containing all variables referenced in formula.

k

Integer, number of neighbours for each base learner. Default 5.

num_base_learners

Integer, number of base learners in the ensemble. Default 10.

num_features_per_base_learner

Integer or NULL (all predictors). Number of predictors drawn at random for each base learner.

metric

Distance, "mahalanobis" (default) or "euclidean" (on standardized columns).

weighting_function

Function mapping a vector of non-negative distances to non-negative neighbour weights. Default: constant weights.

replace

Logical; sample rows with replacement for each base learner. Default TRUE.

sample_fraction

Optional numeric in (0, 1]; fraction of rows drawn for each base learner. Defaults to 1 when replace = TRUE and 0.6321 otherwise.

Value

An object of class "mlsurv_model" with elements:

model

The fitted ensemble: design information, time grid and the base learners (row indices, columns and whitening maps).

learner

Scalar "bnnsurv".

engine

Scalar "survalis".

formula, data

Inputs preserved for downstream use.

time, status

Character names of the survival outcome fields.

Method

Each base learner \(b = 1, \dots, B\) draws a bootstrap (or subsample) of the training rows and, optionally, a random subset of the predictors. For a new observation \(x\), the learner finds the \(k\) training rows closest to \(x\) and returns their weighted Kaplan-Meier curve $$\hat S_b(t \mid x) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{\sum_i w_i \delta_i 1\{T_i = t_j\}} {\sum_i w_i 1\{T_i \ge t_j\}}\right),$$ with weights \(w_i = w(d(x, x_i))\). The ensemble prediction is the average \(\hat S(t \mid x) = B^{-1} \sum_b \hat S_b(t \mid x)\), a non-increasing step function in \(t\). Training rows tied with the \(k\)-th nearest distance share the remaining neighbour slots equally, so predictions do not depend on the row order of the data.

The Mahalanobis distance uses the covariance \(\Sigma_b\) of the base learner's own sample: \(d(x, y)^2 = (x - y)^\top \Sigma_b^{+} (x - y)\), where \(\Sigma_b^{+}\) is the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse. Constant and collinear columns (for example a dummy that never varies in a bootstrap sample) therefore contribute nothing instead of breaking the inversion. metric = "euclidean" uses the Euclidean distance on standardized columns.

Differences from bnnSurvival: factors are one-hot encoded (not coded as integer labels) and new data reuse the training levels; feature subsets are drawn from all predictors (a factor counts as one predictor); constant columns are detected from the variances; prediction runs in the current process (no forking); and predictions at arbitrary times are read off the step function rather than linearly interpolated. With numeric predictors, all predictors per learner, constant weights and no tied distances, the two engines give the same curves for the same seed.

References

Lowsky DJ, Ding Y, Lee DKK, McCulloch CE, Ross LF, Thistlethwaite JR, Zenios SA (2013). A K-nearest neighbors survival probability prediction method. Statistics in Medicine, 32(12), 2062-2069. doi:10.1002/sim.5673

See also

predict_bnnsurv(), tune_bnnsurv()

Examples

mod <- fit_bnnsurv(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age + karno + diagtime + prior,
  data = veteran
)
head(predict_bnnsurv(mod, newdata = veteran[1:5, ], times = c(50, 100)))
#>   t=50 t=100
#> 1 0.82  0.28
#> 2 0.98  0.62
#> 3 0.72  0.34
#> 4 0.78  0.78
#> 5 0.94  0.94
